title: Light Articulation
learningGoals: Keep words clear in a short phrase

sections.heading: Welcome and what we will explore
sections.narration:
Welcome. Today we are exploring Light Articulation. You prepare to say a name and notice your lips or jaw pressing harder than the sound seems to need.

We will notice contact and extra pressure, explore a smaller comfortable effort, and keep words clear in a short phrase. First I will explain the distinction. Then you will see and hear a demonstration, try a few short phrases, and notice your own experience. We will finish with a short prepared rehearsal and an everyday next step. You can pause or ask a question at any point. A small comfortable experiment is enough.

sections.heading: What this tool means
sections.narration:
Articulation means the movements and contacts that shape speech sounds. Contact is not a fault to eliminate. The experiment is whether extra pressing can become smaller while the word stays clear. This differs from voice onset and does not require watching every mouth movement during a conversation.

Your lips, tongue and jaw help shape speech. Today we will compare comfortable contact with extra pressure. Light does not mean barely moving your mouth or whispering. You can form a clear sound while exploring how much effort is actually needed. Use a small difference rather than trying to relax every muscle at once.

Notice the distinction: Light concerns added pressure, not removing the movements that shape a clear sound. You are choosing one feature for this learning experience, rather than inspecting every aspect of speech. We will use short familiar messages so there is room to notice that feature.

sections.heading: Watch and listen
sections.narration:
Watch the demonstration before trying. We will use this message: My name is here on the list. First listen to the models and notice the feature being compared. The labels on screen identify each version. You can replay either model without copying an uncomfortable contrast.

Now listen once more for the message itself. Contact pressure and intelligibility, not whether you produced the lightest possible movement. This is an invitation to compare your experience, not a demand to match the model exactly. When you are ready, move to a short guided attempt.

sections.heading: Try the three small steps
sections.narration:
Let us try this in small steps. First: Notice lip contact in a comfortable M sound. Next: Try a familiar word with gentle contact and an ordinary release. Then: Use the word in a short message without monitoring every contact.

Use these familiar phrases one at a time: My name is here on the list. Please bring the paper. I would like to make a point. Stop between attempts when you want to. You can listen to a model again, record a short attempt, or leave this part to return later. Keep attention on this one chosen feature; you do not need to check every sound. If the attempt becomes effortful, stop and return to comfortable ordinary speaking.

sections.heading: Compare and check
sections.narration:
Consider what this tool is asking you to explore. What does light articulation mean? You can select an answer and read or hear the explanation. It is a check of the idea, not a test of how you sound.

After the check, notice one observation from your attempt: Contact pressure and intelligibility, not whether you produced the lightest possible movement. It is possible for a movement to feel different while the message still takes effort, or for you to be unsure what changed. You can record that uncertainty without repeating until you obtain a preferred result.

sections.heading: From a phrase to your own message
sections.narration:
Choose a short message you actually want to share. You might use one of the phrases we have practised and add one useful detail in your own words. Give yourself one small cue from the demonstration, then let the message continue. There is no need to increase the amount of the technique to make the attempt count.

After speaking, ask what you noticed about the chosen feature and about the message. You can keep a small useful change, adjust it, or leave the result open. Try another short message only if it serves your learning today.

sections.heading: Your observation and next step
sections.narration:
Before finishing, save one observation. Here is the feature we explored: Contact pressure and intelligibility, not whether you produced the lightest possible movement. Something may have changed, things may have felt much the same, or you may be unsure. Your observation belongs to this attempt and setting.

In focused practice, you can deliberately explore this one feature. In conversation, give most of your attention to the message and the other person. A familiar support can be available if it helps; it does not need to become a checklist you monitor throughout the exchange.

Choose one manageable situation in which you would like to speak. You can plan a small practice, have a conversation, revisit the demonstration, or finish here. Save what you would keep, change or leave open.
